analysis.one_liner: Limits each defendant in an injury lawsuit to paying only its own share of damages.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past a Senate subcommittee and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the long-standing rule of joint and several liability, any defendant found responsible for an injury can be made to pay the full judgment when other responsible parties cannot pay. This bill would replace that rule: each defendant would pay only its own percentage of responsibility, unless defendants acted together to cause the harm. If an injured person settled with one defendant for less than its share, or a responsible party was never sued, the injured person's total recovery would be cut by that party's share. The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, then to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses and professionals facing injury lawsuits — the 'deep pocket' defendants, such as manufacturers, insurers, and employers — gain the most. They would no longer be forced to cover the entire judgment when other at-fault parties are broke, unknown, or quietly let off the hook, capping their worst-case exposure at their own percentage share.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Corporate and insurance defendants in injury lawsuits

how_it_helps.text: Each defendant would be liable only for the damages allocated to its own percentage of responsibility, with a separate judgment for that amount, unless defendants engaged in concerted action to cause the harm.
If a claimant released any defendant or potential defendant from liability, the total recovery would be reduced by that party's share of responsibility.
A defendant could point to non-parties it proves caused the harm and have their shares counted against the claimant's recovery.

analysis.who_pays: Injured people whose injury was caused by several parties. Under the bill, any unpaid share of a judgment — because a responsible defendant is insolvent, cannot be found, or was released in an earlier settlement — falls on the injured person rather than on the defendants who could pay.
analysis.who_pays_short: Injured people left with uncompensated damages

drawbacks.text: When one responsible party is insolvent, cannot be joined, or was released by the claimant, the injured person's total recovery is reduced by that party's proportion of responsibility, leaving the shortfall with the victim rather than the solvent defendants.

The exception for 'concerted action' is narrow — it covers only conscious and intentional joint action and excludes consciously parallel conduct — so many multi-actor injuries would still leave the injured person without full compensation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would make litigation more predictable for businesses by ending 'deep pocket' verdicts, which supporters argue unfairly concentrates liability on defendants with money. The cost lands squarely on people who have been injured: they would absorb any shortfall whenever a co-responsible party is broke, gone, or settled with cheaply, reducing total compensation in exactly the cases — multi-defendant accidents, toxic exposures — where proving everyone's share is hardest.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, then to a subcommittee, and sat there with no hearing or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Larry Pressler introduced the Joint and Several Liability Reform Act of 1991 in the Senate on January 14, 1991.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.
On January 24, 1991, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Courts and Administrative Practice, and the record shows no further action of any kind.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The outcome favored injured people, who kept the existing rule that lets them collect a full judgment from solvent defendants. The bill's prospective beneficiaries — corporate and insurance defendants — got nothing, but neither did its sponsor.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured people, who kept full-collection rights

for.name: Sen. Larry Pressler
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate; it drew no cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and the bill had no cosponsors, so there is no record of partisan support or opposition.

industries.industry: Businesses facing tort liability (manufacturers, chemical, pharmaceutical, and other deep-pocket defendants)
industries.note: The bill would have limited their maximum liability to their own percentage share of fault, sparing them from covering judgments when other responsible parties cannot pay. Had it passed, the cost of those shortfalls would have shifted to injured people; its death leaves the existing full-collection rule in place.
By capping any one defendant's exposure, the bill would have reduced insurers' worst-case payouts on multi-defendant claims. It died without action, so their exposure is unchanged.
